html:
The ever-normal granary was a Chinese state system of grain stores used to keep grain prices steady. The state bought grain when harvests were good and prices low, stored it, and sold it when harvests failed and prices rose.

The idea is older than the name. Thinkers of the Warring States period, such as Li Kui of the state of Wei, proposed buying and selling grain to protect both farmers and townspeople. Under the Han dynasty, in 54 BCE, the official Geng Shouchang set up granaries called changpingcang, "ever-normal granaries", in the frontier regions.

Later dynasties revived the system again and again. It was at its largest under the Qing, whose network of granaries helped fight famine in the 1700s.

The idea travelled far. In the 1930s the American agriculture secretary Henry A. Wallace read about it and borrowed the name "ever-normal granary" for the farm policy of the New Deal. Today it is known as a buffer stock scheme.
sum: The ever-normal granary was a Chinese state system of grain stores used to keep grain prices steady. The state bought grain when harvests were good and prices low, stored it, and sold it when harvests failed and prices rose.
